text:
Consider the following compound (X)


[IMG]


The most stable and least stable carbon radicals, respectively, produced by homolytic cleavage of corresponding $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bond are :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Removing H from each labelled carbon of $\mathrm{HC}\equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3})-\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ gives four carbon radicals.

Radical II is secondary and propargylic: the unpaired electron on C-II is delocalised into the adjacent $\mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{C}$ $π$ bond by resonance, so it is the most stable.

$\mathrm{HC}\equiv \mathrm{C}-\dot{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_{3})_{2}⟷\mathrm{H}\dot{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_{3})_{2}$

Radical III is tertiary and is stabilised only by hyperconjugation and the $+I$ effect of the alkyl groups, which is weaker than resonance; radical IV is primary and less stable still.

Radical I is formed on the $sp$ carbon of the terminal alkyne. The unpaired electron occupies an $sp$ orbital (50% $s$-character) that lies along the $\mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{C}$ axis, perpendicular to both $π$ bonds, so it cannot be delocalised; the $sp$ C–H bond is also the strongest C–H bond in the molecule. Radical I is therefore the least stable.

Stability order: II > III > IV > I, so the most and least stable radicals are II and I.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text:
$\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}(\mathrm{s})+2\mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq})\to \mathrm{CaCl}_{2}(\mathrm{aq})+\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$

Consider the above reaction, what mass of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$ will be formed if 250 mL of 0.76 M HCl reacts with 1000 g of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ ?

(Given : Molar mass of $\mathrm{Ca},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{O},\mathrm{H}$ and Cl are $40,12,16,1$ and $35.5\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$, respectively)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The reaction is: 

$\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}(\mathrm{s})+2\mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq})\to \mathrm{CaCl}_{2}(\mathrm{aq})+\mathrm{CO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$

Calculate Moles of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$:

The molar mass of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ is calculated as 

$40+12+3\times 16=100\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{mol}$

Given 1000 g of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$, the number of moles is 

$\frac{1000}{100}=10\mathrm{moles}$

Calculate Moles of $\mathrm{HCl}$:

Using the given concentration and volume for $\mathrm{HCl}$, the moles are calculated as follows:

$0.76\times \frac{250}{1000}=0.19\mathrm{moles}$

$\mathrm{HCl}$ is the limiting reagent (L.R.) because it has fewer moles than needed to completely react with the $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$.

Calculate Moles of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$ Formed:

According to the stoichiometry of the reaction, 2 moles of $\mathrm{HCl}$ produce 1 mole of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$. Therefore, the moles of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$ formed are:

$\frac{0.19}{2}=0.095\mathrm{moles}$

Calculate Mass of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$:

The molar mass of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$ is:

$40+2\times 35.5=111\mathrm{g}/\mathrm{mol}$

Thus, the mass of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$ is:

$0.095\times 111=10.545\mathrm{g}$

Hence, the mass of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$ formed is 10.545 g.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text:
If equal volumes of $AB_{2}$ and $XY$ (both are salts) aqueous solutions are mixed, which of the following combination will give a precipitate of $\mathrm{AY}_{2}$ at 300 K ?
(Given $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}(~$ at 300 K ) for $\mathrm{AY}_{2}=5.2\times 10^{-7}$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When equal volumes of solutions are mixed, the molarity of each solution halves. To determine if a precipitate will form, calculate the ionic product $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}$ using the formula:

$\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}=\left [\mathrm{A}^{2+}\right ][\mathrm{Y}^{-}]^{2}$

A precipitate of $\mathrm{AY}_{2}$ will form if $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}>\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{SP}}$, where $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{SP}}$ is given as $5.2\times 10^{-7}$.

Option D Calculation:

$\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}=\left (1.8\times 10^{-3}\right )\left (\frac{5}{2}\times 10^{-4}\right )^{2}=\text{Calculated value}<\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{SP}}$

Option A Calculation:

$\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}=\left (10^{-4}\right )\left (0.4\times 10^{-3}\right )^{2}=\text{Calculated value}<\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{SP}}$

Option B Calculation:

$\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}=\left (10^{-2}\right )\left (10^{-2}\right )^{2}=\text{Calculated value}>\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{SP}}$

Option C Calculation:

$\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}=\left (\frac{1.5}{2}\times 10^{-4}\right )\left (\frac{1.5}{2}\times 10^{-3}\right )^{2}=\text{Calculated value}<\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{SP}}$

From the calculations, the solution in Option B will form a precipitate since the ionic product $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{SP}}$ is greater than the solubility product $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{SP}}$.

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement (I) : The metallic radius of Al is less than that of Ga .

Statement (II) : The ionic radius of $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is less than that of $\mathrm{Ga}^{3+}$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Radii (pm): metallic radius Al 143, Ga 135; ionic radius $\mathrm{Al}{}^{3+}$ 53.5, $\mathrm{Ga}{}^{3+}$ 62.

Statement I: Ga has ten 3d electrons, which shield the nuclear charge poorly, so its outer electrons feel a larger effective nuclear charge and its metallic radius (135 pm) is smaller than that of Al (143 pm). Statement I is incorrect.

Statement II: $\mathrm{Ga}{}^{3+}$ ($[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}$) has one more electron shell than $\mathrm{Al}{}^{3+}$ ($[\mathrm{Ne}]$), so $\mathrm{Al}{}^{3+}$ (53.5 pm) is smaller than $\mathrm{Ga}{}^{3+}$ (62 pm). Statement II is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
Choose the correct tests with respective observations.

(A) $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}$ (acidified with acetic acid) $+\mathrm{K}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]\to$ Chocolate brown precipitate.

(B) $\mathrm{FeCl}_{3}+\mathrm{K}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]\to$ Prussian blue precipitate.

(C) $\mathrm{ZnCl}_{2}+\mathrm{K}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$, neutralised with $\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{OH}\to$ White or bluish white precipitate.

(D) $\mathrm{MgCl}_{2}+\mathrm{K}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]\to$ Blue precipitate.

(E) $\mathrm{BaCl}_{2}+\mathrm{K}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]$, neutralised with $\mathrm{NaOH}\to$ White precipitate.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In acetic acid medium, $\mathrm{Cu}{}^{2+}$ gives chocolate-brown copper(II) hexacyanoferrate(II), so test A is correct:

$2~\mathrm{CuSO}{}_{4}+\mathrm{K}{}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]\longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}{}_{2}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]↓+2\mathrm{K}{}_{2}\mathrm{SO}{}_{4}$

$\mathrm{Fe}{}^{3+}$ gives Prussian blue, so test B is correct:

$4~\mathrm{FeCl}{}_{3}+3\mathrm{K}{}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]\longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe}{}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}_{3}↓+12\mathrm{KCl}$

$\mathrm{Zn}{}^{2+}$ in neutralised solution gives a white or bluish-white precipitate, so test C is correct:

$3~\mathrm{ZnCl}{}_{2}+2\mathrm{K}{}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]\longrightarrow \mathrm{K}{}_{2}\mathrm{Zn}{}_{3}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}_{2}↓+6\mathrm{KCl}$

$\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}$ gives no blue precipitate with $\mathrm{K}{}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]$ (a blue precipitate with this reagent is the test for $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{3+}$); $\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}$ is confirmed as white $\mathrm{MgNH}{}_{4}\mathrm{PO}{}_{4}$ with $\mathrm{Na}{}_{2}\mathrm{HPO}{}_{4}$ in ammoniacal medium. Test D is incorrect.

$\mathrm{Ba}{}^{2+}$ is not identified with $\mathrm{K}{}_{4}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]$; it is confirmed as yellow $\mathrm{BaCrO}{}_{4}$ with $\mathrm{K}{}_{2}\mathrm{CrO}{}_{4}$. Test E is incorrect.

Only tests A, B and C are correct.

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text: A solution is made by mixing one mole of volatile liquid $A$ with 3 moles of volatile liquid $B$. The vapour pressure of pure A is 200 mm Hg and that of the solution is 500 mm Hg . The vapour pressure of pure B and the least volatile component of the solution, respectively, are:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given:

1 mole of volatile liquid A

3 moles of volatile liquid B

Vapor pressure of pure A, $P_{A}^{o}=200$ mm Hg

Vapor pressure of the solution, $P_{S}=500$ mm Hg

We apply Raoult's law, which states:

$P_{S}=P_{A}^{o}\cdot X_{A}+P_{B}^{o}\cdot X_{B}$

Where:

$X_{A}$ is the mole fraction of A

$X_{B}$ is the mole fraction of B

$P_{B}^{o}$ is the vapor pressure of pure liquid B

Calculate the mole fractions:

$X_{A}=\frac{1}{1+3}=\frac{1}{4}$

$X_{B}=\frac{3}{1+3}=\frac{3}{4}$

Plug these into the equation:

$500=200\times \frac{1}{4}+P_{B}^{o}\times \frac{3}{4}$

Simplifying:

$500=50+\frac{3}{4}P_{B}^{o}$

Subtract 50 from both sides:

$450=\frac{3}{4}P_{B}^{o}$

Multiply both sides by $\frac{4}{3}$ to solve for $P_{B}^{o}$:

$P_{B}^{o}=600\text{mm Hg}$

Since $P_{A}^{o}<P_{B}^{o}$, liquid A is the least volatile component.

In conclusion:

The vapor pressure of pure B, $P_{B}^{o}$, is 600 mm Hg.

The least volatile component is A.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text: A molecule with the formula $\mathrm{AX}_{4}\mathrm{Y}$ has all its elements from p-block. Element A is rarest, monoatomic, non-radioactive from its group and has the lowest ionization enthalpy value among $\mathrm{A},\mathrm{X}$ and Y . Elements X and Y have first and second highest electronegativity values respectively among all the known elements. The shape of the molecule is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Element A is a monoatomic p-block element, so it is a noble gas; the rarest non-radioactive noble gas (radon is radioactive) is xenon.

Fluorine and oxygen have the highest and second-highest electronegativities, so X = F and Y = O, and the molecule is $\mathrm{XeOF}{}_{4}$.

The first ionization enthalpy of Xe (about $1170\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) is lower than that of O ($1314\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) and F ($1681\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$), which agrees with the data.

In $\mathrm{XeOF}{}_{4}$, Xe forms four Xe–F bonds and one Xe=O bond and keeps one lone pair, so it has 6 electron pairs ($\mathrm{sp}^{3}\mathrm{d}^{2}$, octahedral arrangement).

With five bonded atoms and one lone pair, the shape of the molecule is square pyramidal.


[IMG]

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement (I) : In octahedral complexes, when $\Delta _{0}<\mathrm{P}$ high spin complexes are formed. When $\Delta _{0}>P$ low spin complexes are formed.

Statement (II) : In tetrahedral complexes because of $\Delta _{t}<P$, low spin complexes are rarely formed.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In octahedral complexes, which have a coordination number (CN) of 6, the formation of high spin or low spin complexes depends on the relative magnitude of the crystal field splitting energy, denoted as Δ₀, and the pairing energy (P.E.):

If Δ₀ is less than the pairing energy (Δ₀  P.E.), low spin complexes are formed.

In tetrahedral complexes, where the coordination number is 4:

The crystal field splitting energy (Δₜ) is typically less than the pairing energy (Δₜ < P.E.), resulting in the formation of mainly high spin complexes. Low spin complexes are rarely observed in tetrahedral coordination due to this energy consideration.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text: On complete combustion 1.0 g of an organic compound $(\mathrm{X})$ gave 1.46 g of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and 0.567 g of $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$. The empirical formula mass of compound $(\mathrm{X})$ is $__________ g. ($Given molar mass in $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\mathrm{C}:12,\mathrm{H}:1,\mathrm{O}:16$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Calculate the Moles of Carbon:

Carbon is fully converted to $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$.

Moles of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}=\frac{1.46\text{g}}{44\text{g/mol}}=0.033\text{mol}$.

Moles of Carbon ($\text{C}$) = Moles of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ = 0.033 mol.

Mass of Carbon = $0.033\times 12\text{g/mol}=0.396\text{g}$.

Calculate the Moles of Hydrogen:

Hydrogen is fully converted to $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$.

Moles of $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}=\frac{0.567\text{g}}{18\text{g/mol}}=0.0315\text{mol}$.

Moles of Hydrogen ($\text{H}$) = $2\times 0.0315=0.063\text{mol}$.

Mass of Hydrogen = $0.063\times 1\text{g/mol}=0.063\text{g}$.

Calculate the Mass of Oxygen:

Total mass of compound $\mathrm{X}$ = 1.0 g.

Mass of Oxygen = Total mass - (Mass of Carbon + Mass of Hydrogen) 

Mass of Oxygen = $1.0\text{g}-(0.396\text{g}+0.063\text{g})=0.541\text{g}$.

Moles of Oxygen ($\text{O}$) = $\frac{0.541}{16}=0.0338\approx 0.033\text{mol}$.

Determine the Empirical Formula:

The ratio of moles: $\text{C}=0.033$, $\text{H}=0.063$, $\text{O}=0.033$.

Simplified, this ratio is approximately 1:2:1.

Empirical formula: $\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{O}$.

Calculate the Empirical Formula Mass:

Empirical formula mass = $12\times 1+1\times 2+16\times 1=30\text{g/mol}$.

Therefore, the empirical formula mass of compound $\mathrm{X}$ is 30 g/mol.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I : Vanilin 
[IMG]
 will react with NaOH and also with Tollen's reagent.

Statement II : Vanilin 
[IMG]
 will undergo self aldol condensation very easily.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Vanillin is 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde. Its phenolic $-\mathrm{OH}$ is acidic, so it reacts with NaOH to form the sodium phenoxide, and its $-\mathrm{CHO}$ group is oxidised by Tollens' reagent, depositing silver. Statement I is correct.

Self aldol condensation requires an $α$-hydrogen, on the carbon next to the carbonyl group, to form an enolate. In vanillin the $-\mathrm{CHO}$ group is attached directly to a ring carbon that carries no hydrogen, so no enolate forms and vanillin cannot undergo self aldol condensation. Statement II is incorrect.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text: According to Bohr's model of hydrogen atom, which of the following statement is incorrect?
options: Radius of $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit is four times larger than that of $2^{\text{nd}}$ orbit
Radius of $8^{\text{th}}$ orbit is four times larger than that of $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit
Radius of $6^{\text{th}}$ orbit is three times larger than that of $4^{\text{th}}$ orbit
Radius of $3^{\text{rd}}$ orbit is nine times larger than that of $1^{\text{st}}$ orbit
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In Bohr’s model the radius of the $n$th orbit is  

$r_{n}=n^{2}a_{0}$  

where $a_{0}$ is the Bohr radius.  Hence for any two orbits $m$ and $n$:  

$\frac{r_{m}}{r_{n}}=\frac{m^{2}}{n^{2}}.$  

Let’s check each option:

A: $\dfrac{r_{4}}{r_{2}}=\dfrac{4^{2}}{2^{2}}=\dfrac{16}{4}=4$ → correct  

B: $\dfrac{r_{8}}{r_{4}}=\dfrac{8^{2}}{4^{2}}=\dfrac{64}{16}=4$ → correct  

C: $\dfrac{r_{6}}{r_{4}}=\dfrac{6^{2}}{4^{2}}=\dfrac{36}{16}=2.25\left (\neq 3\right )$ → incorrect  

D: $\dfrac{r_{3}}{r_{1}}=\dfrac{3^{2}}{1^{2}}=9$ → correct  

Therefore the incorrect statement is Option C.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text: Identify the correct statement among the following :
options: All naturally occurring amino acids except glycine contain one chiral centre.
Amino acid, cysteine can easily undergo dimerisation due to the presence of free SH group.
Glutamic acid is the only amino acid that contains a $-$COOH group at the side chain.
All naturally occurring amino acids are optically active.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To clarify the statements regarding amino acids:

Chirality in Amino Acids: Most naturally occurring amino acids contain at least one chiral center, but there are exceptions. For example, Isoleucine has two chiral centers, and Glycine is an exception as it is optically inactive due to lacking a chiral center.

Cysteine and Dimerization: The amino acid Cysteine can easily undergo dimerization. This is due to its free sulfhydryl (SH) group, which can form disulfide bonds, leading to the formation of a dimer.

Carboxyl Groups in Amino Acids: Glutamic acid is not the only amino acid with a carboxyl group in its side chain. Aspartic acid also contains a carboxyl group in its side chain.

Optical Activity: While many naturally occurring amino acids are indeed optically active, Glycine is an exception as it does not possess a chiral center and is hence optically inactive. 

In summary:

Not all naturally occurring amino acids are optically active (e.g., Glycine).

Not all naturally occurring amino acids contain only one chiral center (e.g., Isoleucine has two).

Both Glutamic acid and Aspartic acid contain side chain carboxyl groups.

Cysteine can dimerize due to its SH group.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift

text:
The correct order of basic nature in aqueous solution for the bases 

$\mathrm{NH}_{3},\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{NH}_{2},\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{CH}_{2}\mathrm{NH}_{2},(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{CH}_{2})_{2}\mathrm{NH}$ and $(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{CH}_{2})_{3}\mathrm{N}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In water the basic strength of an amine is set by three effects together: the $+I$ effect of the alkyl groups, hydrogen-bond solvation of the protonated amine, and steric hindrance to that solvation.

For ethyl amines the larger $+I$ effect of three ethyl groups outweighs the poorer solvation of $(\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}){}_{3}\mathrm{NH}{}^{+}$, so the aqueous order is $(\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}){}_{2}\mathrm{NH}>(\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}){}_{3}\mathrm{N}>\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$ (pKb 3.00, 3.25, 3.29). This differs from the methyl series, where $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$ is stronger than $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}){}_{3}\mathrm{N}$.

All three ethyl amines are stronger bases than $\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}$ (pKb 4.75), whose nitrogen carries no electron-releasing group.

In hydrazine, $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$, the electronegative $-\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$ group withdraws electron density from the other nitrogen ($-I$ effect), so hydrazine (pKb about 6) is a weaker base than ammonia.

$\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}<\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}<\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}<(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}){}_{3}\mathrm{N}<(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}){}_{2}\mathrm{NH}$

Option (B) places $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}){}_{3}\mathrm{N}$ below $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$, which is the methyl-series pattern and does not apply to ethyl amines.

Note: NTA's answer key for this question gives (B), with $(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}){}_{3}\mathrm{N}<\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$. The NCERT $pK_{b}$ values above make triethylamine the stronger base of the two, so (C) is kept.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
The property/properties that show irregularity in first four elements of group-17 is/are

(A) Covalent radius

(B) Electron affinity

(C) Ionic radius

(D) First ionization energy

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The order of first four elements of group-17 are as follows.

$\mathrm{F}<\mathrm{Cl}<\mathrm{Br}<\mathrm{I}\text{(Covalent radius)}$

$\mathrm{Cl}>\mathrm{F}>\mathrm{Br}>\mathrm{I}$ (Electron affinity)

$\mathrm{F}^{-}<\mathrm{Cl}^{-}<\mathrm{Br}^{-}<\mathrm{I}^{-}$ (Ionic radius)

$\mathrm{F}>\mathrm{Cl}>\mathrm{Br}>\mathrm{I}$ ( $\mathrm{I}^{\mathrm{st}}$ ionization energy)

Electron affinity order is irregular.

text:
For the reaction A $\to$ products.


[IMG]


The concentration of A at 10 minutes is $_________$ $\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{mol}\mathrm{L}^{-1}$ (nearest integer). The reaction was started with $2.5\mathrm{mol}\mathrm{L}^{-1}$ of A .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Order of Reaction:

Since $t_{1/2}\propto [A]_{0}$, the reaction follows a zero-order kinetics.

Half-life Equation for Zero-order Reaction:

The half-life ($t_{1/2}$) is calculated as:

$t_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2K}$

Given the slope from the graph is $76.92$, which equals $\frac{1}{2K}$. This implies:

$K=\frac{1}{2\times 76.92}$

Concentration of A at 10 Minutes:

Apply the zero-order kinetics equation:

$[A]_{10}=-Kt+[A]_{0}$

Substituting the values:

$[A]_{10}=-\left (\frac{1}{2\times 76.92}\right )\times 10+2.5=2.435\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Final Concentration:

Convert to scientific notation:

$[A]_{10}=2435\times 10^{-3}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Thus, the concentration of A at 10 minutes is approximately $2435\times 10^{-3}\text{mol L}^{-1}$.

text:
Consider the following electrochemical cell at standard condition.

$\mathrm{Au}(\mathrm{s})|\mathrm{QH}_{2},\mathrm{Q}|\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{X}(0.01\mathrm{M})||\mathrm{Ag}^{+}(1\mathrm{M})|\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}=+0.4\mathrm{V}$

The couple $\mathrm{QH}_{2}/\mathrm{Q}$ represents quinhydrone electrode, the half cell reaction is given below:


[IMG]

$\left [\text{Given :}\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}}^{0}=+0.8\mathrm{V}\text{and}\frac{2.303\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{F}}=0.06\mathrm{V}\right ]$

The $\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{b}}$ value of the ammonium halide salt $(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{X})$ used here is $__________ . ($nearest integer)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The quinhydrone electrode is on the left, so it is the anode, and the silver electrode is the cathode:

Anode: $\mathrm{QH}{}_{2}\qquad \longrightarrow \mathrm{Q}+2\mathrm{H}{}^{+}+2\mathrm{e}{}^{-}$

Cathode: $2~\mathrm{Ag}{}^{+}+2\mathrm{e}{}^{-}\longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Ag}$

Cell reaction: $\mathrm{QH}{}_{2}\qquad +2\mathrm{Ag}{}^{+}\longrightarrow \mathrm{Q}+2\mathrm{H}{}^{+}+2\mathrm{Ag}$, with $n=2$.

$E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }=E_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}}^{\circ }-E_{\mathrm{Q}/\mathrm{QH}_{2}}^{\circ }=0.8-0.7=0.1\text{V}$

With $[\mathrm{Ag}{}^{+}]=1\text{M}$ and Q and $\mathrm{QH}{}_{2}$ at unit activity, the Nernst equation gives

$E_{\text{cell}}=E_{\text{cell}}^{\circ }-\dfrac{0.06}{2}\log \dfrac{[\mathrm{H}{}^{+}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{Ag}{}^{+}]^{2}}=0.1-0.06\log [\mathrm{H}{}^{+}]=0.1+0.06\text{pH}$

$0.4=0.1+0.06\text{pH}\Rightarrow \text{pH}=5$

$\mathrm{NH}{}_{4}\mathrm{X}$ is a salt of a weak base and a strong acid, so for its $0.01\text{M}$ solution

$\text{pH}=7-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{p}K_{b}-\dfrac{1}{2}\log C$

$5=7-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{p}K_{b}-\dfrac{1}{2}\log (10^{-2})=8-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{p}K_{b}\Rightarrow \text{p}K_{b}=6$

Hence, the answer is 6.

text:
Consider the following equilibrium,

0.1 mol of CO along with a catalyst is present in a $2\mathrm{dm}^{3}$ flask maintained at 500 K . Hydrogen is introduced into the flask until the pressure is 5 bar and 0.04 mol of $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}$ is formed. The $K_{p}^{θ}$ is $__________$ $\times 10^{-3}$ (nearest integer).

Given : $\mathrm{R}=0.08\mathrm{dm}^{3}$ bar $\mathrm{K}^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Assume only methanol is formed as the product and the system follows ideal gas behaviour.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]


$\begin{array}{l} V=2L \\ T=500K \\ P_{\text{total}}=5\text{bar} \\ n_{\text{Total}}=0.25=\dfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{mol} \\ P_{\text{total}}=n_{\text{total}}\times \dfrac{RT}{V} \\ \Rightarrow 5=(0.06+a-0.08+0.04)\times \dfrac{0.08\times 500}{2} \\ \Rightarrow 10=(0.02+a)\times 0.08\times 500 \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=0.25-0.02=0.23\mathrm{mol} \\ \begin{array}{l} \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{P}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}}}{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{CO}}\times \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{H}_{2}}^{2}}\times \dfrac{1}{(\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{T}})^{2}}=\dfrac{0.04}{0.06\times (0.15)^{2}}\times \left [\dfrac{1/4}{5}\right ]^{2} \\ =\dfrac{4}{6\times (0.15)^{2}\times 16}\times \dfrac{1}{25} \\ =\dfrac{100\times 100}{24\times 225\times 25}=\dfrac{100\times 100}{135000} \\ =0.074=74\times 10^{-3} \end{array} \end{array}$

text: A transition metal (M) among $\mathrm{Mn},\mathrm{Cr},\mathrm{Co}$ and Fe has the highest standard electrode potential $\left (\mathrm{M}^{3+}/\mathrm{M}^{2+}\right )$. It forms a metal complex of the type $[\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]^{4-}$. The number of electrons present in the $\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{g}}$ orbital of the complex is $___________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The standard electrode potentials $E^{\circ }(\mathrm{M}{}^{3+}/\mathrm{M}{}^{2+})$ are: Cr $-0.41\text{V}$, Fe $+0.77\text{V}$, Mn $+1.57\text{V}$ and Co $+1.97\text{V}$. Co has the highest value, so M = Co.

The complex is $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{4-}$, in which cobalt is $\mathrm{Co}{}^{2+}$ with configuration $3d^{7}$.

$\mathrm{CN}{}^{-}$ is a strong-field ligand, so $\Delta _{o}$ exceeds the pairing energy and the electrons pair in $t_{2g}$ before entering $e_{g}$: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{1}$.


[IMG]

Hence, the answer is 1.
